By only returning `true` for `&&` and `||`, the nullish coalescing operator will be handled more like a conditional (it will only fork once at the point of checking for nullish, rather than “boolean-fork” for all falsy values).

With this change in place, when you analyze `(a && b) ?? c` you’ll now get three distinct paths:

  1. `a` is truthy, then evaluate `b`, then short–circuit through `??` (skipping `c`)  
  2. `a` is falsy (but not nullish), skip `b` and short–circuit through `??` (skipping `c`)  
  3. `a` is nullish, skip `b` and take the right side of `??`, i.e. evaluate `c`  

which matches the actual runtime behavior of `(a && b) ?? c`.
